title: Olaparib for prostate cancer
context_label: BRCA1/2-mutated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after a new hormonal agent
indication_text: BRCA1/2-mutated metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after a new hormonal agent
purpose: Help control prostate cancer that has progressed despite hormone treatment, where a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation is confirmed.
schedule_summary: The usual starting dose is 300 mg of olaparib tablets twice daily, with or without food, continuously while helpful and tolerable. Kidney function, interactions or side effects can change the prescribed dose. This prostate course does not use the one-year breast or two-year ovarian limit.

monitoring_summary: Full blood count, kidney and liver tests every four weeks for the first 12 months, then as clinically indicated. Persistent low counts after an interruption may need specialist blood investigations. Review new cough, breathlessness, bleeding and leg swelling promptly.
safety_note: Follow your own prescription and hospital instructions. This information supports a discussion; it does not authorise treatment.
urgent_extra: Call your oncology team promptly for fever, shaking chills, feeling suddenly unwell, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting/diarrhoea or new breathlessness. Follow your own temperature and contact plan. Severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, collapse, seizures or stroke symptoms: call 112/999.

agents.name: Olaparib
agents.mechanism: Olaparib blocks poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which helps repair damaged DNA. A cancer cell with a pathogenic BRCA1/2 change already has difficulty using another repair pathway. Blocking PARP can leave too much damage for the cell to survive. This is why a validated mutation result matters.
agents.explanation: Olaparib blocks poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP), which helps repair damaged DNA. A cancer cell with a pathogenic BRCA1/2 change already has difficulty using another repair pathway. Blocking PARP can leave too much damage for the cell to survive. risks: Anaemia, sometimes requiring transfusion; low white cells and platelets with infection or bleeding
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, indigestion, reduced appetite and taste changes
Fatigue, weakness, headache, dizziness and mouth soreness
Serious or persistent blood-count changes; rare myelodysplastic syndrome or acute myeloid leukaemia, sometimes fatal
New cough or breathlessness from pneumonitis, which can be serious or fatal
Blood clots in veins or lungs; seek urgent help for a swollen leg, chest pain or breathlessness
Liver injury and changes in kidney blood tests; organ function and interactions may require dose changes
Allergic reactions, possible fertility effects and harm to an unborn child
agents.watch: NCCP classes oral olaparib as moderate-to-high sickness risk. The team considers anti-sickness medicine and a proton pump inhibitor for stomach protection under local policy. Obtain a written prevention/rescue plan and report persistent nausea or inability to take tablets.

anatomy: Fatigue is common and may also signal anaemia. Report marked weakness, dizziness or symptoms affecting daily life.
Taste changes, soreness and poor appetite may make eating difficult. Ask early for symptom and nutrition support.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment for infection, inflammation or a clot. Severe symptoms need emergency care.
Tests guide safe dosing. Report yellow skin/eyes, dark urine or much less urine.
Take prescribed sickness support. Call if vomiting or diarrhoea persists, you cannot drink, or pain is severe.
Low cells may cause breathlessness, infection or bruising. Rare persistent marrow problems need specialist investigation.
Report unusual bruising, bleeding, fever, shivers or suddenly feeling unwell. Do not wait for the next blood test.
A new painful swollen leg needs urgent assessment. Sudden chest pain or severe breathlessness is an emergency.

support.title: Preparation and symptom support
support.text: Confirm the pathogenic germline or tumour BRCA1/2 result and previous treatment. Continue prescribed androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) unless you have had surgical castration. support.title: Safe medicine use
support.text: Swallow tablets whole; do not chew, crush, dissolve or divide them. Tablets and capsules are not interchangeable. If a dose is missed, take the next normal dose at its usual time; never double up. Avoid grapefruit and Seville oranges, and check all medicines with pharmacy.

support.title: Fertility and contraception
support.text: Use a condom during treatment and for three months afterwards when having sex with a partner who is or could become pregnant. The partner should use highly effective contraception during that time. Do not donate sperm during treatment or for three months afterwards; discuss fertility preservation.

support.title: Your wider treatment
support.text: Continue ADT, which keeps testosterone low, unless you have had surgical castration. Olaparib targets DNA repair rather than replacing hormone suppression. Abiraterone and other androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) act on hormone signalling; adding or switching them needs a separate evidence-based plan. Radiotherapy can treat selected sites or relieve symptoms, with timing agreed by the team.

items.title: Evidence in this setting
items.text: In the BRCA1/2-mutated subgroup of PROfound, 160 patients received olaparib or the investigator’s choice of abiraterone or enzalutamide after progression on a new hormonal agent. Median radiological progression-free survival was 9.8 versus 3.0 months (hazard ratio 0.22; 95% confidence interval 0.15–0.32); median overall survival was 20.1 versus 14.4 months (hazard ratio 0.63; 0.42–0.95). These subgroup analyses were not controlled for multiple comparisons. They do not compare every modern alternative or establish the separate olaparib-plus-abiraterone regimen.

items.title: Fertility and contraception

The partner should use highly effective contraception during that time. Do not donate sperm during treatment or for three months afterwards; discuss fertility preservation.

items.title: Your priorities
items.text: Discuss benefit, burden, alternatives including supportive care, and choosing to decline or stop treatment. Trial averages cannot predict your own outcome.
